clue.text: Due to conflict over the middle of the Red Sea ahead

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letter, the only one kept

blocks.note: for can mean because of, as in 'for that reason'
a war is an armed conflict
the central letter of Red
S is the abbreviation for sea

explanation.surface: Because of fighting in the Red Sea region, a ship presses on.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' means placed above, so the conflict goes before the letter from Red.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving in the direction one faces is going onward, toward the front.

clue.text: Tough end cut off vegetable

indicators.note: cutting off an end removes a letter from one extremity, here the front

blocks.note: chard is a leafy vegetable

explanation.surface: A cook trims the stringy end off a tough vegetable.
explanation.definitionFit: Firm, resistant to pressure, difficult to chew or break are all senses of the adjective.

clue.text: Contemptible but delectable, showing no resistance

indicators.note: showing no of something means that thing is absent, so its letter is taken out

blocks.note: scrummy is British informal for delicious
R is the physics symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: Something despicable yet delicious, offering no resistance.
explanation.definitionFit: Being worthless, low and despicable is like being covered in filthy surface froth.

clue.text: Pursue aliens: ask ‘even this is futile?’

indicators.note: even picks out the letters at even positions, the second, fourth and so on

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth letters and so on of these three words

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether chasing extraterrestrials is pointless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Even' reads like 'even this', a shrug, but it selects letters at even positions.
explanation.definitionFit: Something futile achieves nothing, serving no purpose at all.

clue.text: Really minced its oaths

indicators.note: mincing chops something up finely, so these letters are cut up and reassembled

blocks.note: the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Someone truly softened their swearing, using minced oaths.
explanation.walkthrough: A minced oath is a softened curse such as 'gosh'; here 'minced' is the scrambling signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Said as an exclamation of surprise or doubt, 'Really?' and this phrase are interchangeable.

clue.text: Woman rings boy to collect rustic drink

indicators.note: to ring something is to encircle it, so one piece wraps round the rest

blocks.note: a dame is a woman
a son is a boy
to collect a prize is to win it

explanation.surface: A woman phones her son to pick up some country drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A homemade country wine from small dark plums is a traditional rural tipple.

clue.text: Leaders of hominids, usually making a nuisance somewhere?

definitions.text: Leaders of hominids, usually making a nuisance somewhere?

indicators.note: the leaders of a set of words are their opening letters

blocks.clueFragment: hominids, usually making a nuisance somewhere
blocks.note: the first letter of each of these six words

explanation.surface: The top members of a primate family are always being a pest somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as a wry description: we are the hominid line, and a nuisance wherever we go.
explanation.definitionFit: People are the leading hominids, and the question mark admits the cheeky claim that we are pests everywhere.

clue.text: Leaders of first revolution in crash …

indicators.note: a revolution turns things over, so the letters of the next word are spun into a fresh order

blocks.note: Monday, the first day of the week, abbreviated; it starts the chain of days that the across clues' 'next' follows
the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: The heads of the first uprising are caught up in a collapse.
explanation.walkthrough: This clue opens a running theme: in the across clues each 'next' is the following day of the week, starting from MON here, then TUE, WED and so on, wrapping round twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Kings and queens are rulers of their realms, so they are national leaders.

clue.text: … way before next bust, perhaps …

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for street
A is short for ante, Latin for before
the day after Monday from the previous clue, abbreviated

explanation.surface: A road comes ahead of the next collapse, continuing the dotted chain of clues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' looks like a positional word but supplies its own letter, A for ante; 'next' is Tuesday, following MON in 8 across.
explanation.definitionFit: A bust is a sculpted head and shoulders, one kind of carved figure or sculpture.

clue.text: … fearful of acting next

blocks.note: A is a standard abbreviation for acting, as in a job title
the day after Tuesday from the previous clue, abbreviated

explanation.surface: Someone is nervous about going on stage next.
explanation.definitionFit: To be struck with wonder mixed with dread is to feel reverential fear.

clue.text: Critical of population growth: wild animals taking over next

indicators.note: wild suggests running out of control, so the letters of the following word are scrambled
to take something over is to hold it within, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: the anagram fodder
the day after Wednesday from the previous clue, abbreviated

explanation.surface: A warning that untamed beasts are overrunning things, as population booms.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Malthus argued that population growth would outrun the food supply; his followers and ideas take his name.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes the economist Thomas Malthus's gloomy view that unchecked human numbers outstrip resources.

clue.text: Next target for the ambitious and spirited

blocks.note: the day after Thursday from the previous clue, abbreviated
the ambitious aim for the sky, which is proverbially the limit

explanation.surface: The next goal for go-getters with plenty of drive.
explanation.definitionFit: Lively, playful and full of energy are all ways of saying high-spirited.

clue.text: Badly stung, I go in bawling

indicators.note: badly suggests things done wrongly, so the letters are jumbled into another order

blocks.note: the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Painfully stung, someone goes indoors howling.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling or shouting loudly is a way of crying out at full volume.

clue.text: Next heretical saint, Lucifer’s follower

indicators.note: a heretical view departs from the accepted order, so the word that follows is rearranged

blocks.note: the day after Friday from the previous clue, abbreviated
the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A holy figure gone heretical turns into a devotee of the devil.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucifer is another name for the devil, and one who worships the devil is a devotee of him.

clue.text: After start of assembly, next socialist moving to Left separately

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept
in an across clue moving leftwards means reading the word from right to left

blocks.note: first letter of assembly
the day after Saturday from the previous clue, abbreviated
a red is a socialist or communist

explanation.surface: At a meeting, a left-winger drifts further left and the group splits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the assembly letter first, ahead of the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: To be torn apart into pieces means things now stand apart from one another.

clue.text: Rejoicing in extravagance, raised by parent, ultimately a six-footer

indicators.note: in a down clue raising a word lifts it upward, so it reads bottom to top
ultimately points to the final letter of the word before it

blocks.note: luxe is luxury or lavishness
last letter of parent
an insect has six legs, and an ant is one

explanation.surface: A tall child brought up in luxury is delighted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Six-footer' suggests a tall person, but a footer here is a foot, and six feet means an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: Being triumphantly joyful and jubilant is the same as rejoicing.

clue.text: Maintain surveillance over next terrible riot

indicators.note: something terrible is a mess, so the letters of the following word are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: the week wraps round: the day after Sunday is Monday, abbreviated
the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Police keep watch over the next dreadful disturbance.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to keep watch on something continuously, checking its progress.

clue.text: A joke describing the Titanic, for example

blocks.note: first meaning: a quip delivered in a single sentence
second meaning: the Titanic was a single ocean liner

explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words, the phrase simply describes the ship: it was one passenger liner.
explanation.definitionFit: A short quip told in one line is a stock comic form, while the ship was a single passenger vessel.

clue.text: Station on the Oxted line where one second is painful, time slipping away

indicators.note: a letter slipping away drifts out of its place, so the word's order changes

blocks.note: a means one
S is the abbreviation for second
something that hurts is painful

explanation.surface: A commuter's grumble about a station where a moment hurts while time ticks away.
explanation.walkthrough: The time letter in the painful word slides to the end. Ashurst is a village station in Kent on a branch of the Oxted line south of London.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a small railway stop served by Southern trains on the route through Oxted.

clue.text: Patrons of hospital: Boatman (Boatman!) next to join society

blocks.note: H is the map and sign abbreviation for hospital
an AB, able seaman, is a sailor, a boatman
Boatman is also the setter, who refers to himself as I
the day after Monday from the previous clue, abbreviated
S is a standard abbreviation for society

explanation.surface: The setter, with comic insistence on his own name, joins the regulars at a hospital society.
explanation.walkthrough: The name appears twice for two different letter groups: once as an ordinary sailor, once, with the exclamation, as the setter himself.
explanation.definitionFit: Regular visitors to a place, such as a bar or club, are its habitual customers.

clue.text: Gay porn stash discovered: they keep the blood flowing

indicators.note: dis-covered words have lost their covers, the first and last letters of each

blocks.note: Gay without its outer letters
porn without its outer letters
stash without its outer letters

explanation.surface: A hidden stash of racy material is found.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discovered' seems to mean found, but read as dis-covered it strips each word's ends.
explanation.definitionFit: These main arteries carry oxygenated blood from the heart round the body.

clue.text: Country’s next dash

blocks.note: the possessive ending supplies its own letter
the day after Tuesday from the previous clue, abbreviated
an en is a short printer's dash, the en dash

explanation.surface: A nation's next hurried move.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s looks like a possessive or 'is' joining definition to wordplay, but it gives a letter of its own.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a Scandinavian kingdom, so it names a nation.

clue.text: People used to call for these to bear them, but some ceased answering

definitions.text: People used to call for these to bear them

indicators.note: some means only a portion of the following words is taken, a run of letters within them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: Folk once summoned these to carry them, though some no longer reply.
explanation.walkthrough: Sedan chairs were enclosed seats carried on poles by two bearers, hired like taxis in the 18th century.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedan chairs were summoned in the street to carry passengers, so people once called for them.

clue.text: Boatman’s cell, harsh at first, next emerged empty and vividly coloured

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter of the word it follows
an empty word has lost its contents, leaving only its outside letters

blocks.note: a brig is a prison cell on a ship, fitting for a boatman
first letter of harsh
the day after Wednesday from the previous clue, abbreviated
the outside letters of emerged

explanation.surface: The setter tells of leaving a harsh prison cell, coming out into a brightly coloured world.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a brilliant hue means showing strong, intense colour.

clue.text: Next ton of material for glass

blocks.note: the day after Thursday from the previous clue, abbreviated
T is the abbreviation for ton

explanation.surface: The next tonne of raw stuff for glassmaking.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the calcined mixture of sand and fluxes fused to make glass or glaze.

clue.text: Report of having taken part in battles – here

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: having taken part in battles means having fought

explanation.surface: An account of battles waged at this very spot.
explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British speech the two words sound identical. 'Here' points at the place where the battles were fought.
explanation.definitionFit: A stronghold is a likely place where battles were waged, the location the clue points to.

clue.text: A place in the heavens for next to win, say

indicators.note: say signals that the words before it are to be heard, not spelt

blocks.note: the day after Friday from the previous clue, abbreviated
to win is to earn, and earn has the same sound as a vase for ashes

explanation.surface: Someone hopes to win a place in heaven next.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a planet, a body occupying its own position in the night sky.

clue.text: Odds and ends from next drains

blocks.note: the day after Saturday from the previous clue, abbreviated
to drain something of liquid is to dry it

explanation.surface: Bits and pieces fished out of the next drains.
explanation.definitionFit: Miscellaneous small items too minor to list separately are assorted bits and pieces.
